resident.chief_complaint: Progressive weakness and clumsiness of extremities with significant gait disturbance; unable to walk for 2 years without help.
resident.history: A 67-year-old man reported progressive weakness and clumsiness of his extremities and significant gait disturbance. He had been unable to walk for 2 years without help.
resident.physical_exam: Examination showed a severe spastic-ataxic gait, severe paresis of the upper extremities, almost complete loss of fine movements of both hands, significantly elevated reflexes, severe foot clonus, and Babinski sign bilaterally. Functional scores: mJOA 5, Nurick 4.
key_positive_signs: Almost complete loss of fine movements of both hands
resident.past_history: Smoker. No other past medical history documented.
resident.public_message: A 67-year-old man, a smoker, presented with progressive weakness and clumsiness of the extremities and significant gait disturbance; he had been unable to walk without help for 2 years. Examination revealed severe spastic-ataxic gait, severe paresis of the upper extremities, almost complete loss of fine movements of both hands, significantly elevated reflexes, severe foot clonus, and Babinski sign bilaterally (mJOA 5; Nurick 4). MRI showed intervertebral disc protrusions at C3–C4, C4–C5, C5–C6, and C6–C7, posterior osteophytes at C4–C5–C6–C7 causing compression of the spinal cord and corresponding radixes, and a T2 hyperintensity at the C5 and C6 vertebrae. No separate laboratory report is provided.

imaging.public_message: Reporting the case record's description of the imaging; the films were not available for review. The record describes multilevel ventral spinal cord and root compression from disc protrusions at C3-4 through C6-7, with posterior osteophytes from C4 through C7. T2 hyperintensity is reported at the C5 and C6 vertebral levels. Stenosis severity was not stated. These reported findings correlate highly with the described myelopathic symptoms.

neurology.localization: Findings localize to the cervical spinal cord, most likely between C3 and C6, with bilateral corticospinal tract involvement producing hyperreflexia, clonus, Babinski, and spasticity. The severe upper limb paresis and loss of fine hand movements suggest dysfunction of the cervical enlargement, but the absence of lower motor neuron signs (e.g., atrophy, hyporeflexia) places the lesion above the C5–T1 anterior horn cells or reflects upper motor neuron predominance. The ataxic component of gait is consistent with posterior column involvement at the same level, though sensory examination is not documented. Multilevel compression from C3–4 through C6–7 could account for the findings, and a single level cannot be confidently excluded.

red_flags.finding: The physical examination report does not document sensory testing (e.g., proprioception, vibration, pinprick) or sphincter function, despite the spastic-ataxic gait and upper limb paresis.
red_flags.rationale: This absence limits precise attribution of the ataxic component (sensory vs spastic) but offers no alternative explanation for the dominant cervical myelopathy; multilevel cord compression with T2 signal remains the clear cause, so it does not alter the indication or plan.

neurology.public_message: The clinical findings localize to the cervical spinal cord (C3–C6) with bilateral corticospinal tract signs and likely posterior column involvement. Imaging shows multilevel ventral cord compression at C3–4 through C6–7 with T2 hyperintensity at C5–6, which explains the dominant syndrome; match level is high. One coexisting red flag is noted: the examination record lacks sensory and sphincter testing, so the sensory component of the ataxia cannot be fully evaluated, but this does not change the indication for addressing the cervical compression.

anesthesia.public_message: ASA physical status III. Intraoperative mean arterial pressure target 85 mmHg. Blood loss risk unassessable because the operative plan is not specified. Prone position tolerance is assessed as low. Extubation difficulty is unassessable because no airway assessment is documented.

preconditions_for_failure: No improvement in mJOA or Nurick scores by 3 months of strict conservative therapy
Any neurologic deterioration during the treatment period, including new sphincter dysfunction or worsening gait
Development of new myelopathic symptoms or progression on imaging
Patient inability to participate meaningfully in rehabilitation
physiatrist_opening.public_message: This patient has severe cervical myelopathy (mJOA 5, Nurick 4) with cord compression and T2 signal change. While surgery is strongly indicated given the severity and progression, I put forward a structured 3–6 month conservative trial as a real option, with the understanding that the success rate for meaningful improvement without surgery in such severe cases is approximately 20%. This trial would include intensive physical therapy, core strengthening, posture management, and close neurologic monitoring. Surgery should be pursued if any of the preconditions for failure are met. I acknowledge the evidence against delaying surgery in severe myelopathy, but I hold that a carefully monitored conservative trial may be justified if the patient prefers to avoid immediate operation.

physiatrist_final.public_message: The Deputy Director put forward the T2 signal change and multilevel compression as grounds for immediate surgery, but these are the same findings I have already weighed. T2 signal change in severe myelopathy is associated with poorer prognosis with conservative care, which is exactly why I set a high bar for failure and limited the trial to 3–6 months with close monitoring. However, no new finding in the record—such as acute deterioration, sphincter involvement, or worsening imaging—has been presented that would outweigh the patient's right to choose a structured conservative trial if he prefers to avoid immediate operation. I hold my position.

vice_opinions.assessment: Severe multilevel cervical spondylotic myelopathy (mJOA 5, Nurick 4) with T2 hyperintensity at C5–6, correlating with ventral cord compression from disc/osteophyte at C3–4 through C6–7. Surgical decompression is indicated; a conservative trial is not supported given the severity and myelomalacia. The main unresolved issues are the choice of surgical approach and the extent of fusion, which require direct review of the imaging and knowledge of sagittal alignment.
proposed_options: Anterior cervical decompression and fusion (ACDF) from C3 to C7, with corpectomy at the levels of dominant ventral compression if necessary.
Posterior cervical decompression and fusion (laminectomy C3–C7 with lateral mass fixation) if sagittal alignment is lordotic and no dominant ventral compression.
Conservative management with 3–6 months of supervised rehabilitation and close monitoring, accepting high risk of irreversible deterioration.
vice_opinions.preferred_option: Anterior cervical decompression and fusion (ACDF) from C3 to C7, with corpectomy at the levels of dominant ventral compression if necessary.
disagreement_points: The structured conservative trial proposed by the physiatrist is not appropriate for severe myelopathy with T2 signal change; delaying surgery risks irreversible neurological decline.

The choice between anterior and posterior decompression cannot be settled without reviewing the actual MRI; the sagittal alignment and whether the compression is dominantly ventral will dictate the approach.

There is uncertainty about whether the C3–4 level requires inclusion; the reported disc protrusion at C3–4 may or may not be compressing the cord significantly, and this affects the extent of surgery.
deferred_questions_to_director: Do you agree that we should not offer a conservative trial, given the severity?
After reviewing the imaging, which decompression approach would you favor—anterior, posterior, or combined—and what is your assessment of the sagittal alignment?
Should we obtain additional imaging (CT, flexion/extension) or consult an otolaryngologist if anterior approach is considered?
vice_opinions.public_message: I assess this as severe multilevel cervical myelopathy with T2 signal change, and I believe surgery is mandatory; I do not see a defensible role for a 3–6 month conservative trial given the risk of irreversible damage. My preferred operation is an anterior decompression and fusion from C3 to C7 to directly address the ventral compression, but I recognize that posterior fusion could be reasonable if the films show lordosis without dominant ventral compression. I have not personally reviewed the MRI, so I need your judgement on the imaging and the final approach. Should we proceed with surgery without a trial, and do you favor anterior or posterior decompression?

director_rulings.final_decision: Surgery is indicated. I reject the structured conservative trial proposed by the physiatrist: severe myelopathy with T2 signal change and progressive disability carries unacceptable risk of irreversible damage. I agree with the Deputy Director that anterior decompression is the preferred first-line approach, but the final construct will be confirmed after review of the actual MRI and additional imaging. We will proceed with surgery on the following plan, with contingencies as stated.
director_rulings.surgical_plan: Anterior cervical decompression and fusion from C3 to C7, with corpectomy at levels of dominant ventral compression if necessary. Contingencies: (1) if MRI demonstrates lordosis with primarily dorsal compression, switch to posterior decompression and fusion; (2) if C3-4 disc protrusion is not significantly compressing the cord, limit fusion to C4-C7; (3) if flexion/extension radiographs show instability, add posterior fusion or consider combined approach.
delegated_tasks: Radiologist: review the actual MRI films and report sagittal alignment, degree of compression at each level (especially C3-4), and extent of T2 hyperintensity.
Anesthesiologist: perform an airway assessment and document intraoperative positioning plan.
Resident: obtain the patient's current medication list, smoking history, and clarify his preference after explaining the risks and benefits; also document baseline sensory and sphincter function.
director_rulings.public_message: Thank you all. Dr. Resident, please clarify the patient's current functional status and his expressed preference after hearing the risks. Dr. Radiologist, please review the actual MRI films and report sagittal alignment, degree of compression at each level, and extent of T2 hyperintensity. Dr. Anesthesiologist, please perform an airway assessment and report your positioning plan. Based on the discussion, I rule that surgery is indicated. I reject the proposal for a 3-6 month conservative trial due to severe myelopathy with T2 signal change and the risk of irreversible damage. I agree with the Deputy Director that anterior decompression is preferred, but the final approach will be confirmed after the requested imaging. The provisional plan is ACDF C3-C7 with corpectomy at dominant compression levels if needed, with the following contingencies: if MRI shows lordosis and dorsal compression, we switch to posterior fusion; if C3-4 is not significantly compressive, we limit to C4-C7; if instability is present on flexion/extension, we add posterior fusion. Please obtain detailed informed consent from the patient and family. We will proceed with preop CT and flexion/extension films today, and I will schedule a brief reconvening after imaging to finalize the approach.
